items.title: Commission Delegated Regulation (EU) 2017/589, Article 12: Kill functionality
items.quote: An investment firm shall be able to cancel immediately, as an emergency measure, any or all of its unexecuted orders
items.why: Source of the quotation. Assimilated law applying to investment firms engaged in algorithmic trading, not to AI in general: the one UK rule found that requires an immediate stop. legislation.gov.uk shows it up to date to 30 September 2026 and lists a revocation by the Financial Services and Markets Act 2023, Sch. 1 Pt. 3, as not yet applied. The regulator's own pages on any replacement rules were not read.

items.title: Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 (AI Act), Article 14: Human oversight
items.publisher: European Commission, AI Act Service Desk
items.quote: interrupt the system through a 'stop' button or a similar procedure that allows the system to come to a halt in a safe state
items.why: International comparator. High-risk systems must be provided so that the people overseeing them can intervene or interrupt them. A duty on providers of high-risk systems only. Article 26(5), same site, requires deployers to suspend use where the system presents a risk. The Commission's copy, not the Official Journal (EUR-Lex returned an empty page). The page carries a notice that the provision was amended by the Digital Omnibus on AI and the text shown is not yet updated. Article 113 on the same site, shown as consolidated at 27 July 2026, gives 2 December 2027 and 2 August 2028 as the dates from which these sections apply.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence Risk Management Framework (AI RMF 1.0), NIST AI 100-1
items.publisher: National Institute of Standards and Technology
items.locator: Table 4, MANAGE 2.4, p. 32; Table 1, GOVERN 1.7, p. 23
items.quote: to supersede, disengage, or deactivate AI systems that demonstrate performance or outcomes inconsistent with intended use
items.why: The clearest framework statement of the control: mechanisms in place and applied, with responsibilities assigned and understood. Voluntary US framework; no legal force in the UK.

items.title: Code of Practice for the Cyber Security of AI
items.publisher: Department for Science, Innovation and Technology
items.quote: System Operators should ensure that a known good state can be restored.
items.why: The UK code does not use the words kill switch or off switch. What it has: tested incident and recovery plans (6.5), disaster recovery tailored to attacks on AI (5.3), a known good state that can be restored (5.3.1, a 'should'), and technical measures where human oversight is a risk control (4.3). Voluntary.

items.title: Implementation Guide for the AI Cyber Security Code of Practice
items.publisher: Department for Science, Innovation and Technology
items.locator: Provision 5.3, PDF p. 26; Principle 4, PDF p. 21
items.quote: disable automated responses temporarily while restoring integrity
items.why: The worked examples: a fallback that switches off automated responses, manual backup processes while a model is restored, and an override control on a chatbot that can take actions. Explanatory, not a requirement.

items.title: Guidelines for secure AI system development: Secure design
items.locator: Section 'Design your system for security as well as functionality and performance'
items.quote: you apply appropriate restrictions to the possible actions (this includes external AI and non-AI fail-safes if necessary)
items.why: Basis for designing containment before deployment where a system can trigger actions such as amending files or sending output to other systems. Guidance, not a rule.

items.title: LLM06:2025 Excessive Agency
items.quote: Utilise human-in-the-loop control to require a human to approve high-impact actions before they are taken.
items.why: Practitioner measures that limit damage before a stop is needed: least functionality, least permission, human approval, rate limiting. Community consensus document, not a standard. No publication date is shown on the page.

items.title: How are AI agents used? Evidence from 177,000 MCP tools
items.locator: Abstract on the AI Security Institute research page
items.quote: the share of 'action' tools rose from 27% to 65% of total usage over the 16-month period sampled
items.why: Source of the figure. 177,436 agent tools created from November 2024 to February 2026, drawn from public repositories; software development accounts for 67% of them, so the figure describes that population, not all business use. Only the abstract on the Institute's page was read.

items.title: Cyber Governance Code of Practice
items.publisher: Department for Science, Innovation and Technology
items.locator: Principle D (incident planning, response and recovery)
items.quote: Gain assurance that the organisation has a plan to respond to and recover from a cyber incident impacting business critical technology processes, information and services.
items.why: The board-level expectation that a response and recovery plan exists; the next action in the same principle asks for it to be exercised at least annually. Not specific to AI. Voluntary.

items.title: Quantifying Frontier LLM Capabilities for Container Sandbox Escape
items.locator: Abstract on the AI Security Institute research page
items.quote: when vulnerabilities are added, LLMs are able to identify and exploit them
items.why: Evidence that the isolation used to contain AI agents has to be tested, not assumed. A benchmark result under test conditions; only the abstract on the Institute's page was read.
